https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-russia-tra.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OWm6 Kyiv's ability to defend against Russian drones and missiles has been reportedly limited after Elon Musk's Starlink restricted its speed for Ukraine's military Image: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Russia and Ukraine traded major attacks overnight, authorities from both countries said on Thursday, shortly after US envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg. Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, wounding tens of residents, city authorities said. In an update later in the morning, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had fired 21 missiles towards 12 regions in Ukraine. In Kyiv region, the strikes killed two people and injured 34 others, including five children. The subway infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro river in Kyiv was also damaged, Mayor ⁠Vitali ​Klitschko ​said ​on Telegram. Ukraine's airforce warned of Russian missiles and instructed residents to take shelter Image: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance "Overnight, Kyiv residents heard what Russian 'humanism' truly sounds like: a brutal attack with dozens of ballistic missiles striking energy infrastructure, medical facilities, shopping centers, and residential Areas," Ukrainian foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media. His post referred to Witkoff recently calling Putin a "humanitarian" for freeing US citizen Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday. Hubbard had been captured by Russian forces and jailed over charges of being a mercenary. The Ukrainian foreign minister added: "Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will." Another Russian strike killed a woman and injured four others in the Kharkiv region in northeast Ukraine, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram. A drone also hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure in the Poltava region, local authorities said without providing more details. Russia faces hundreds of drones Meanwhile, Russia's Defense Ministry said it downed 808 Ukrainian drones overnight, with many targeting Moscow. At least two people were killed in the Ukrainian strikes on Russia. In western Russia's Lipetsk city, a man was injured as drones hit apartment buildings and a medical facility, Governor Igor Artamonov said on Telegram. Strikes after US attempts mediation The latest round of strikes came after US special envoy Witkoff held talks with Zelenskyy in Norway earlier this week , followed by talks with Putin in Russia on Wednesday. The Trump administration has attempted to mediate between the two sides to end the conflict that began with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. US aims for new round of Russia-Ukraine negotiations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Putin agreed "in principle" to resume US-mediated peace talks with Kyiv as soon as next month. Zelenskyy, too, said on Wednesday that Ukraine supported a US proposal for trilateral talks at the negotiators level to be held as soon as possible. It was "the closest we've been" to ending the war, US President Donald Trump claimed after Witkoff's meeting with Putin. However, that did not stop the neighboring nations from keeping up a barrage of attacks. "Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening," Zelenskyy said in a post on social media on Thursday. "It is important to keep trying to find the right solutions to end this war. But when Russia responds to negotiations with ballistic missiles, real pressure on Russia is needed to bring about different steps – steps toward ending the killing," he said, once again advocating for stronger air defense capabilities and a faster supply of missiles from allies. Photograph: Youpla View image in fullscreen The Youpla Group collapsed in March 2022, leaving more than 13,000 Aboriginal people without the means to pay for funerals. Photograph: Youpla Youpla/ACBF funeral fund Youpla directors disqualified over collapsed funeral fund that targeted Aboriginal families Three directors were fined a combined $90,000 in federal court judgment and disqualified from managing a corporation for between five and 10 years Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Caitlin Cassidy Tue 10 Nov 2026 23.55 EST Last modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 00.23 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three directors of a collapsed funeral fund that marketed insurance to Aboriginal families have been banned from managing corporations for at least five years and ordered to pay a combined $90,000 after being found to have breached their duties to clients. On Wednesday, federal court justice Geoffrey Kennett ordered the former director of the insurance company Youpla Group, previously the Aboriginal Community Benefit Fund (ACBF), Jonathan Law, to pay the commonwealth $50,000 and disqualified him from managing corporations for six years. Michael Wilson, also a director, was ordered to pay $20,000 and disqualified from managing corporations for 10 years, while director Geoffrey Clayton was ordered to pay $20,000 and disqualified from managing corporations for five years. The trio were also ordered to pay a combined $17,000 towards plaintiff’s costs. Kennett found they had failed to perform their duties with the degree of “care and diligence” expected, failed to manage conflicts of interest, and caused a detriment to the ACBF members. About a third of $96m ACBF-Youpla victim support scheme to be spent on administration Read more It followed a judgment late last month where the founder of the company, Ron Pattenden , was ordered to pay a quarter of a million dollars and barred from managing corporations for 15 years. Pattenden acknowledged he had breached directors’ duties in a claim settlement with financial watchdog, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC). During the same judgment, the former Youpla Group chief Bryn Jones was found by Kennett to have breached his directorial duties after a contested liability hearing in February. He denied having knowledge of the fund’s insurance premium increases. Jones’s penalty will be determined at a hearing at a later date. Youpla sold junk funeral policies to Indigenous people across Australia for decades, including targeting communities where English was not the first language and communities with low literacy levels. It collapsed in March 2022, leaving more than 13,000 Aboriginal people, some elderly and in palliative care , without the means to pay for funerals. Families had to resort to crowdfunding and some were forced to leave their loved ones’ bodies in the morgue while they raised the funds. In August 2023, Asic commenced proceedings in federal court against the five former directors and officers for breaches of their duties, alleging governance failures and director misconduct that affected the First Nations people who were members of the funds. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email It alleged the directors and officers maintained insurance arrangements with Crown Insurance, a Vanuatu-based company owned and controlled by Pattenden and another director, Law, and did not act in the best interest of the ACBF entities and members. Breaches of directors’ duties can attract a maximum penalty of $200,000 for each breach that occurred between 2017 and March 2019. Youpla targeted Indigenous people using marketing materials in the distinctive red, black and yellow colours of the Aboriginal flag, including stuffed toys and colouring books for children, turning up to community events and by conducting door-to-door sales. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion It was investigated by various regulators over the years but it was not until 2018, when its conduct was exposed in the banking royal commission, that its licence to sell new products was withdrawn. In 2021 Asic questioned its solvency, and the company’s directors finally pulled the plug. The federal court handed Youpla a $1.2m fine in September 2023 for misrepresenting junk funeral policies, finding it had told plan holders they would receive a lump sum payment when in fact they would only be reimbursed for expenses they could prove had been incurred. Youpla avoided paying millions more in fines handed down by the federal court in July 2025 because it was in liquidation. A $97m federal government support package was announced in February 2024 to help thousands of mostly low-income Aboriginal families recover from financial loss. The government’s payments to remaining victims will continue to be processed until 1 December this year. Eligible recipients have the choice of a funeral bond or a cash payment worth 60% of the value of their policy. – with Australian Associated Press.
